source.title: Varying Shades of Wrong: Aligning LLMs with Wrong Answers Only
source.authors: Ji-Han Yao; Wen-Xuan Ding; Shang-Bin Feng; Lucy Lu Wang; Yulia Tsvetkov

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses weak-to-strong work as related context, but its experiments study preference alignment among wrong answers, not whether a stronger student trained on weaker-model labels beats its supervisor or recovers a performance gap.
record.gate_note: The paper fine-tunes LLaMA3-8B with DPO on wrong-over-wrong preference pairs. Its supervisor/evaluator is often GPT-4o, or the preference source is an oracle or the model's own outputs; it does not test the weak-supervisor/strong-student comparison or report PGR. The adjacent wrong-over-wrong alignment outcomes are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study tests wrong-over-wrong DPO alignment, not weak-to-strong training. It does not train a stronger student on weaker-model labels, and it reports no PGR. In the alignment runs, preferences come from GPT-4o or an oracle and the student is LLaMA3-8B, which is the strong-to-weak direction if anything. Burns et al. (2024) appears only in a related-work list on easy-to-hard generalization, so 'cites_only' fits better than 'discusses'.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors find LLMs can rank wrong answers above chance (up to 70.9% with score-based GPT-4o judging), and that wrong-over-wrong alignment complements right-over-wrong alignment. They also report it was not helpful on domains without clear right-wrong distinctions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses DPO preference optimization on pairs of incorrect answers ranked by wrongness, rather than supervised fine-tuning a stronger model on labels from a weaker supervisor. The main alignment student is LLaMA3-8B.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported wrong-over-wrong alignment gains vary by dataset and preference-generation method; the authors also report sensitivity to hyperparameter selection.

fits_no_version.finding: Wrong-over-wrong DPO alignment of LLaMA3-8B improves average proxy wrongness, accuracy and calibration (0.074, 0.045, 0.044 on average). Gains are larger on open-ended tasks (Bio Generation, NLGraph) and absent on domains without clear right-wrong distinctions (Table 8).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: DPO on preferences between incorrect answers can make a model less wrong, more accurate and better calibrated, depending on the domain.

fits_no_version.finding: A weaker evaluator judges a stronger model's wrong answers well: LLaMA3-8B reaches 0.649 AccWoW on GPT-4o answers, while GPT-4o's accuracy drops when judging its own answers. This concerns judging preferences, not training a student.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weaker LLMs can provide moderately accurate wrong-over-wrong judgements on a stronger model's outputs, sometimes better than the stronger model's self-evaluation.

record.problems: The authors note that correctness proxies are imperfect, results are sensitive to hyperparameter selection, and the tested datasets do not fully represent settings without clear ground truth. The reported aggregate improvements have no uncertainty estimates in the text.
record.rows_left_out: Per-dataset and per-preference-method results in Table 2, and the no-clear-separability results in Table 8, were not extracted because they concern wrong-over-wrong alignment rather than any tested claim version.

untested.parts: No weak supervisor, strong student or strong ceiling; no PGR.
No weak-to-strong training changes compared against naive fine-tuning on weak labels.
No variation of PGR with supervisor or student size, task, or representations.
No weak-to-strong failure modes or distribution-shift effects on PGR. The Table 5 generalization is about wrong-over-wrong alignment, not PGR.
No theory of when a student must beat its supervisor.

record.verdict_notes: The record's peer_reviewed field says ICLR 2024, which looks wrong: the preprint dates from October 2024, so ICLR 2025 is likely; verify. The tranche and the 'none' links are correct; the relation should be cites_only rather than discusses.

versions.untested_parts: No weak-supervisor versus stronger-student comparison; no PGR.
Does not compare changes to weak-to-strong training against naive weak-label fine-tuning.
Does not study PGR variation by supervisor/student size, task, or representations.
Does not test the specified weak-to-strong failure modes or distribution-shift effects on PGR.
No theory of when a student must outperform its supervisor.

relation.reason: Burns et al. appears in the related-work overview of easy-to-hard generalization; the experiments do not test or rely on weak-to-strong generalization.

tranche.reason: The study evaluates wrong-over-wrong preference alignment, without testing or using the finding that a strong student can outperform a weaker supervisor.

source_check.notes: The three averages are explicitly reported, but summarize multiple alignment setups rather than a single configuration. Preferences for the alignment experiments come from GPT-4o or an oracle; no PGR or weaker-supervisor performance comparison is reported.

statements.correction: LLaMA3-8B average improvements: Δpwrong = 0.074; ΔAcc = 0.045; −ΔECE = 0.044. Larger improvements on Bio Generation and NLGraph. Appendix A, Table 8: wrong-over-wrong alignment not universally helpful on SciBench and MedMCQA; some individual accuracy or calibration improvements remain.
statements.problem: The averages and larger open-ended-task improvements are supported. Saying gains were absent without clear right/wrong distinctions overstates mixed results: some accuracy or calibration cells improve.
